THE PHILOMATHEAN SOCIETY.—Information as to the history of the Philomathean Society is scarcer than for the Platonian. But the records of the College show that the Society was actively organized during the years 1884-1885, the Philomathean, and its by-laws show the membership may have changed in those years after after the Platonian Society.

The following item suggests that a friendly rivalry existed between the Platonian and Philomathean Societies:

Plato to Philo—"What is your question for debate at the next regular meeting?"
Philo to Plato—"What is your question for debate at the next regular meeting?"
Plato to Philo—"Touch not, taste not, handle not."

One of the songs of the college drinking song, Krambemball, can roughly be translated as:

It is Lizzie Paxton who carries in the writing an account of the following episode which as well reflects "negativism," as a chore. "I recall that many of the young temperance ladies would sign the pledge."

The pass word was "God loves children," and I remember how deeply it was when I was a little girl at the first meeting. This was when he was in it.

Mrs. Wyatt, wife of a Savoy physician, was the first organized charter of the Platonian Messenger. Both the Philomathean and Platonian were reported in the Platonian Messenger—the Philomathean apparently reported less often—for a period of several years after the College years, a tradition brought over from the College days.

THE GEORGE ELIOT COTERIE.—The beginning of the George Eliot Coterie is told in the following story by its first president, Miss Lizzie Stuff:

The "George Eliot Coterie" was organized through the influence of Prof. Preston D. Caldwell[?] and a few other College graduates at Savoy College. We organized for our motto, "Earth's noblest thing—a woman perfectly trained." Our aim was to lay the foundation stones of a permanent society. Some of the members are:

"We are not united by the difficulties which befall societies. We believe in our friends and daughters and pupils."⁶⁹

⁶⁹Ibid., Vol. III, No. 3, November 1, 1886.
